comment: Reproducible source list for ir/mch_ir.json (the PRODUCTION artifact). Paths are relative to the mch package dir (indexer/indexer/events/mch/). Order == matcher registration order; equal-priority matchers tie-break on this order. specs_decl/jettons.mch (declarative jetton family) and specs_decl/pton_transfer.mch carry in-spec `priority 90` so they register ahead of the priority-100 specs regardless of position, replacing the former 'a_jettons_decl.mch' filename-sort hack. pton_transfer shares the 0x0f8a7ea5 anchor with jetton_transfer and must stay listed AFTER it: the tie-break on this order is what makes a real (internal-leg) transfer get consumed first, mirroring the legacy matchers list. Regenerate: python -m indexer.events.mch.ir_emit --manifest ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir/emit_manifest.json -o ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json (run from indexer/ with the venv python). specs_decl/dedust_v2_swap.mch is listed right after the dedust family and BEFORE the stonfi/tonco swap specs, mirroring the legacy matchers list (dedust_v2.matchers() sits between DedustSwapBlockMatcher and StonfiSwapBlockMatcher); it also anchors on btype jetton_transfer, so it must stay after the priority-90 jetton specs that build those blocks. specs/teleitem_auction.mch sits at its file-name-sort position: neither of its anchors (0x487a8e81 / 0x371638ae) is claimed by another spec, so its position carries no tie-break — it happens to mirror the legacy list, where both Teleitem matchers follow the telegram/getgems nft purchase matchers. specs/nft_mint.mch is listed FIRST and carries in-spec `priority 80`: NftMintBlockMatcher is the FIRST entry of event_processing.matchers, ahead of the priority-90 jetton specs, so it claims a deploying leaf before any jetton/DEX matcher can absorb it — and it is what makes `btype nft_mint` available to specs/tonco_liquidity.mch, which binds it. The three coffee files sit in file-name-sort order, which also mirrors the legacy list's deposit -> swap -> withdraw run (coffee_create_vault rides along in coffee_liquidity.mch, one slot earlier than legacy puts it — unobservable, its 0xc0ffee06 anchor is claimed by nothing else). specs/coffee_withdraw.mch anchors on btype jetton_burn, shared with specs/stonfi_v2_withdraw.mch; the two are structurally disjoint so the tie-break is unobservable despite coffee being listed first. specs/nft_sale.mch (the GetGems sale/auction family) sits AFTER specs/getgems.mch and specs/nft_transfer.mch, which is load-bearing twice: its nft_put_on_sale matcher shares the `btype nft_transfer` anchor with getgems_nft_purchase and must lose that tie-break exactly as the legacy list orders them, and four of its matchers BIND nft_transfer / nft_purchase blocks those two specs produce. Matcher order WITHIN the file also matters — nft_finish_auction is listed before nft_cancel_auction because their anchors overlap on the stop/finish opcodes. specs/dedust_v2_claim_fees.mch sits immediately BEFORE specs/dedust_v2_claim_reward.mch, mirroring dedust_v2.matchers() (claim_fees then claim_reward); their anchors (0x5652f1df / 0x909fdb65) are disjoint, so the tie-break is unobservable. specs/tonstakers.mch carries in-spec `priority 85` on all three of its matchers, which IS observable: its withdraw matcher shares the 0x595f07bc JettonBurn anchor with the priority-90 `jetton_burn`, and legacy registers TONStakersWithdrawMatcher ahead of JettonBurnBlockMatcher, so a default priority let the jetton family eat the anchor and suppressed the whole tonstakers withdraw family. specs/dedust_v2_withdraw.mch is listed right after specs_decl/dedust_v2_swap.mch, mirroring dedust_v2.matchers() (swap, failed swap, withdraw); its 0x20b5ef89 anchor and the three inner opcodes are claimed by nothing else, so the tie-break is unobservable — what matters is only that it stays after the priority-90 jetton specs, whose jetton_transfer blocks are its payout legs. specs/elections.mch sits at its file-name-sort position: neither elector anchor (0x4e73744b / 0x47657424) is claimed by another spec and neither matcher binds a block another matcher produces, so it carries no tie-break at all. The three coffee-tail files (specs/coffee_create_pool.mch, specs/coffee_mev.mch, specs/coffee_staking.mch) are listed LAST, in the legacy matchers-list order (create_pool_creator/create_pool 78-79, mev hold funds 80, staking 82-84). That tail position IS load-bearing for the last two: coffee_mev_protect_hold_funds_jetton and coffee_staking_deposit both anchor on `btype jetton_transfer`, shared with ethena_deposit, jvault_stake, stonfi_v1_swap and dedust_v2_swap/failed_swap, and the legacy list registers all of those AHEAD of the coffee tail — so anything but a position behind them would let a coffee matcher steal an anchor legacy gives to another protocol. coffee_staking_deposit has the widest anchor of the three (a BARE btype jetton_transfer, no where-clause) and is therefore dead last. specs/coffee_create_pool.mch carries no tie-break of its own (0xc0ffee23 is claimed by nothing else) but its two matchers are SERIAL — coffee_create_pool anchors on the `coffee_create_pool_creator` btype the matcher above it produces — so their order WITHIN the file is what makes the pair work. specs/dedust_v2_deposit.mch is listed right after specs/dedust_v2_withdraw.mch, completing the dedust_v2.matchers() mirror (swap, failed swap, withdraw, deposit, rejected deposit, partial deposit); its two anchors (0x25251ee0 / 0xdc5ddba1) are claimed by nothing else, so the file's slot carries no tie-break — what matters is only that it stays after the priority-90 jetton specs, whose jetton_transfer blocks are its deposit carriers and its refund legs. Matcher order WITHIN the file IS load-bearing: final and rejected share the 0x25251ee0 anchor (final first, exactly as the reference lists them) and both consume the 0xdc5ddba1 CreditAsset as a parent, so the partial matcher must stay last or it would claim that parent first. specs/tgbtc.mch grew from one matcher to SEVEN (the mint plus tgbtc_burn, tgbtc_new_key and the four log-only fallbacks); its manifest slot is unchanged and still carries no cross-spec tie-break, but two things about it are now load-bearing. First, matcher order WITHIN the file: each `*_log_only` matcher anchors on an event-log opcode its full sibling CONSUMES (mint eats 0x77a80ef3, burn eats 0xca444ce6, new_key eats both 0x27756729 and 0x453443a6), so the fallbacks must stay last or every complete trace would also emit a crippled `*_fallback` row — the file lists all seven in the legacy matchers-list order (event_processing.py:268-274). Second, tgbtc_burn anchors on `btype jetton_burn`, shared with specs/coffee_withdraw.mch, specs/stonfi_v2_withdraw.mch and the priority-85 tonstakers withdraw: it must stay behind the priority-90 jetton family that BUILDS that block (it does, default priority 100), and its position relative to the other two jetton_burn consumers is unobservable because all three are structurally disjoint (tgbtc needs a 0x7bdd97de/0x587643a2 notify child carrying a 0xca444ce6 log; the other two need their own protocol opcodes) — the same reasoning already recorded for coffee_withdraw vs stonfi_v2_withdraw, and the reason the file may sit after coffee_withdraw here while legacy registers it before. Of the file's nine opcodes only 0x7bdd97de is declared by any other spec (dedust_withdraw, tonstakers, the decl jetton family) and none of them ANCHORS on it. specs/layerzero.mch grew from one matcher to FIVE (the receive plus layerzero_send, layerzero_send_tokens, layerzero_commit_packet and layerzero_dvn_verify); its manifest slot is unchanged and still carries no cross-spec tie-break — none of its twenty-two opcodes is declared by any other spec. Matcher order WITHIN the file is load-bearing for exactly one pair: layerzero_send_tokens anchors on `btype layerzero_send`, the block layerzero_send produces, so it must stay after it. It also binds a `jetton_transfer` PARENT, so it must stay behind the priority-90 jetton family that builds that block (it does, default priority 100). The other three anchors (0x22f3ac09 / 0x28b97077 / 0xa0d51a8d) are pairwise distinct and structurally disjoint, so layerzero_receive keeping its historical first slot rather than the legacy list's third position is unobservable. W4 fixtured singles (2026-07-31) appended one matcher to each of three EXISTING files, and only ONE of the three touches ordering. specs/vesting.mch grew to two matchers (vesting_add_whitelist joining vesting_send_message): its slot carries no tie-break — 0x7258a69b / 0xf258a69b are claimed by nothing else — and the two matchers are independent, neither binding what the other produces. specs/tonco_liquidity.mch grew to three (tonco_deploy_pool listed BETWEEN deposit and withdraw, mirroring event_processing.matchers 64/65/66); 0x2e3034ef and 0x441c39ed are claimed by nothing else and the matcher binds no prebuilt block, so neither its file slot nor its in-file position is load-bearing. specs/ethena.mch grew to two, and its new ethena_withdrawal_request carries in-spec `priority 85`, which IS observable: it anchors on the RAW 0x0f8a7ea5 call and binds the RAW 0x642b7d07 mint, both of which the priority-90 jetton family would otherwise consume into blocks first. The legacy list interleaves them (JettonTransferBlockMatcher 14, ethena withdrawal 48, JettonMintBlockMatcher 49, ethena deposit 50), which one priority per spec file cannot express, so 85 puts the withdrawal ahead of all three jetton matchers instead of between two of them — safe by construction, because the matcher's guards require the internal transfer to land on a jetton MASTER, exactly the shape build_jetton_transfer_core rejects (see the spec header). ethena_deposit keeps the default 100 and therefore still runs after the jetton family that builds the blocks it binds. Within the ethena file the deposit stays listed first, the reverse of the legacy list; unobservable, the two anchors are mutually exclusive. specs/cocoon.mch (2026-07-31) is listed LAST, mirroring event_processing.matchers where the twelve Cocoon matchers are the final twelve entries. The slot is not load-bearing and neither is the default priority 100: all nineteen cocoon opcodes are declared by NO other spec, no cocoon matcher anchors on a btype (so it can neither steal a block another family builds nor depend on one having run), and no cocoon matcher binds a block another cocoon matcher produces — which also makes the in-file order of the twelve free. The two opcode-SET anchors ({0xa040ad28,0xf5f26a36} worker payout, {0x9c69f376,0xfafa6cc1} request refund) are disjoint from each other and from the ten single-opcode anchors; the three opcodes several matchers share (0xc59a7cd3 Payout, 0x2565934c ReturnExcessesBack, 0x65448ff4 ClientProxyRequest) only ever appear as CHILDREN. specs/subscriptions.mch is listed immediately after specs/elections.mch: this mirrors the legacy ElectionRecoverStakeBlockMatcher -> SubscriptionBlockMatcher -> UnsubscribeBlockMatcher sequence. AuctionBidMatcher is represented inside the later grouped specs/nft_sale.mch; the subscription opcodes are unique and neither matcher binds another spec's product, so that unavoidable family grouping makes the slot non-load-bearing.
excluded_note: specs/jetton_transfer.mch and specs/jettons.mch are DELIBERATELY OMITTED (A4). They are builder-tier conformance references (duplicate jetton_transfer/burn/mint matchers of specs_decl/jettons.mch), permanently C++-skipped, and inert in Python (decl-jettons at priority 90 consume the blocks first). Keeping them in the production artifact only produced duplicate/ambiguous name-keyed shadow counters + dead SKIP lines. They stay in specs/ for the Python conformance suite (which references them by matcher name), so suffixing was not an option.
